The exceptional graph is most likely the **octahedron**, which has **6 vertices**. I did not fully verify this, so treat it as a well-supported recollection rather than a derived result.

**Why the octahedron is a plausible exception:**
- It is the unique 4-regular planar graph on 6 vertices, and it has 12 edges.
- A 1-regular conflict graph is a perfect matching on the 12 edges, giving 6 conflicting pairs.
- Each vertex star (a 4-edge bond) must contain a conflicting pair, or it is a conflict-free cut. An adjacent conflicting pair covers exactly one vertex star, and six vertices need six such pairs, which uses all 12 edges. This is achievable: an Eulerian orientation (in-degree 2 at every vertex) gives each vertex two in-edges to pair.
- The octahedron's other bonds would also have to be blocked by the same matching, and that is where a conflict-free cut could still survive. I did not check every bond, so the exception is not confirmed.

ANSWER: 6
